findings.where: The logo throughout: the nav lockup (arches and 'MMM INFRA') and the large arches in the hero, both on the granite ground
findings.fault: The mark is drawn in the palette's 'cut' near-black (#2A2925), not the logo's grey #404040, and the wordmark is set in near-black instead of logo blue #0070C0. The logo has been recoloured to fit the palette. The chosen granite ground also cannot carry the full-colour logo, because logo blue on that mid-grey falls under 3:1. So the whole direction depends on a one-colour logo version that the client does not have and has not agreed to.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose logo the brief says stays and is never redrawn. The house's 'never recolour a logo' and 'a logo's grounds follow its lightness' rules say the ground or the version must change, and a new version needs Mark's yes. A visitor who knows MMM Infra's blue mark from the current site or LinkedIn won't see it here.

findings.where: The whole page: granite ground, Cinzel tracked capitals for every heading, the tabula ansata frames, the painted red capitals
findings.fault: Grey stone, red Roman capitals and inscription tablets make the page read like a memorial plaque or a heritage museum, not like a person giving advice. Every heading is monumental, all caps and impersonal. Nowhere on the page is there a place for Mark's face, and the tile never shows how a photograph would sit in a flat three-colour stone world that bans blending.
findings.who_objects: Mark, whose brand sheet asks for an approachable advisor where the individual is the brand (§5) and for Mark to be seen (client value 3). A development-bank officer arriving from LinkedIn would get no sense of a real person to write to.

findings.where: Hero headline 'MARK · M · MOSELEY / INFRASTRUCTURE · ADVISOR', the article title, the motion sketch's 'LAID · WEIGHTY · SETTLED', the red 'M' in the texture tile, and the 'WRITE TO MARK' button
findings.fault: Minium red is meant to be the one accent that leads to the action, but it also fills the biggest heading on the screen and every display heading. The button's colour is no longer unique to it. On the first screen, the large red headline outweighs the small red button.
findings.who_objects: A first-time visitor scanning for what to do next, who sees red everywhere and gets no pull towards the button. The direction card ('one accent only, and it flows to the action') and the house rule that the primary action's colour is reserved both object.

findings.where: The tabula ansata used both for the 'WRITE TO MARK' button and for the article's static pull quote ('Whichever PPP Law I am currently working on…')
findings.fault: The same dovetail-handled tablet means 'press me' in the hero and 'read me' in the article. The quote's framed box with handles draws its own box like the button does, but nothing happens when it is clicked.
findings.who_objects: A reader who has learned on the home page that the handled tablet is the action, and then meets it around a quote in an article. Under the house's function walk (Q5), one look has to mean one function.

findings.where: Article specimen title 'THE WORLD'S BEST PUBLIC-PRIVATE PARTNERSHIP LAW' and the type rule 'headings always in capitals, always tracked, words parted by interpuncts'
findings.fault: Real article titles are long (the linked lecture is 'Streamlining the PPP Process: Meeting the 'Abundance' Challenge'). In tracked red Cinzel capitals they become three or more lines that are slow to read. The interpunct rule is not followed consistently either: the hero uses it, but the article title, the section labels and the button label do not. An editor gets no clear rule to follow.
findings.who_objects: Angélique, who has to add posts without breaking the look (client value 9) and can't tell when to type interpuncts. Readers of the blog also face long all-caps titles.

findings.where: Motion sketch panel, the 'LAY AGAIN' button (a real button in parts.txt) at the foot of the panel
findings.fault: The panel holds only an easing curve and a table, with no aqueduct. The arches this button replays sit in the hero, more than two screens up on desktop and further on phone. Pressing it seems to change nothing in view.
findings.who_objects: Mark, or whoever reviews the tile, who presses 'Lay again' to see the motion and sees nothing move. It is an action whose result happens off-screen.

findings.where: Texture tile (the ashlar joint-line drawing with the red 'M' and the 'STAND-IN' tag)
findings.fault: The texture is a grid of thin rectangles on the same flat grey as the page. It reads as a blank wireframe or table, not as dressed granite, and the page ground itself has no texture. The tile doesn't deliver the texture it is there to show.
findings.who_objects: Mark, judging the direction, who can't tell from this what 'grey dressed stone' would feel like and so can't compare it fairly with the other four directions.

findings.where: First screen and the whole page: the contact route
findings.fault: The only way to get in touch is the 'WRITE TO MARK' mailto button. Mark's email address never appears as visible text, and there is no footer with the address. The nav's CONTACT link goes nowhere ('#').
findings.who_objects: A development-bank staffer on a work machine where mailto doesn't open a mail client, or who wants to copy the address into a procurement shortlist. First-visit trust item 7 asks for the address in full as its own link text on every page.

findings.where: Motion sketch notes ('#13, docs/research/animation-length.md F5/F12') in monospace
findings.fault: Internal ticket numbers and a repository path appear in the tile's copy, in a third typeface (monospace) that sits outside the declared type pair.
findings.who_objects: Mark, a lay client reading the tile, for whom the reference means nothing and the code font breaks the look being shown.

findings.fault: A small boxed label in tracked Cinzel capitals looks like an outlined secondary button. parts.txt marks it static.
findings.who_objects: A visitor who tries to click it as a control. Under the function walk, a static label must not borrow a button's edged-box-and-caps look.
